entities.summary:
Pheidippides, or Philippides (Ancient Greek: Φιλιππίδης), was a legendary Athenian hemerodromos, or day-runner, whose purported extraordinary long-distance run in 490 BCE became a powerful symbol of Greek defiance and endurance during the Greco-Persian Wars. Though his existence is attested primarily through the later writings of Plutarch and Lucian, it is Herodotus, writing a generation after the events, who recounts a crucial mission undertaken by a runner named Pheidippides, dispatching him from Athens to Sparta to seek military aid against the invading Persian forces. His story, deeply embedded in Western cultural consciousness, transcends its historical ambiguities to represent the ultimate test of human physical and mental fortitude in the service of a greater cause.

According to Herodotus' Histories (Book VI, 105–106), the Athenian polemarch Callimachus and general Miltiades, facing the imminent threat of Darius I's Persian army at Marathon, dispatched Pheidippides to Sparta to request military assistance. This epic journey covered approximately 240 kilometers (150 miles) over rugged terrain, which Pheidippides reportedly completed in less than two days. Upon his arrival in Sparta, he delivered the urgent Athenian plea, only to be informed by the Spartans that their religious customs, specifically the Carneia festival, prevented them from marching until the next full moon. This delay meant Spartan aid would not arrive until after the pivotal Battle of Marathon, fought without their assistance.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Pheidippides holds significant historical importance primarily through his role in inspiring the modern Olympic marathon race, a global athletic event. His legendary, albeit partly apocryphal, acts of endurance in 490 BCE cemented his status as a powerful cultural symbol of perseverance and heroic sacrifice.
